# FLUX

> LLM cost reduction for Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible
> APIs, billed as a percentage of verified savings. Integration is one URL
> (proxy mode) or one line (SDK). Savings are measured per completed task
> with quality held, from the provider's own reported usage, and every
> invoice is recomputable by the customer from a hash-chained event ledger.
> Figures are per traffic segment (one number would be wrong for most
> customers), simulator-measured at providers' published prices: multi-turn
> Claude cache-only 37.6% vs the same prompt-reduction stack without caching
> (both arms clean 38/40); the 57.1% full-stack comparison loses 5 pp clean
> tasks against raw uncached baseline and fails the -2 pp quality limit, so it
> is not a qualified win. Other figures: async/batch 57.7% net, one-shot templated 45.5-72.8%,
> interactive agents 25.9-34.0%, already-optimised stacks 0-5% with an
> explicit do-not-pay-us verdict. The fee is 1% of verified savings,
> monthly, nothing else; a month that saved nothing bills nothing. The latest real-traffic export (30 requests on
> claude-sonnet-5-5) measured 18.0% of live spend billed as verified savings
> across five agents, with the Claude cache lever earning live.

# FLUX — verified LLM cost reduction, billed only on savings you can recompute

FLUX is a drop-in wrapper for your OpenAI or Anthropic client that reduces what
you spend per completed task — and proves it. You pay a percentage of verified
savings. If your traffic is already optimised, FLUX tells you not to pay us.

## What FLUX saves, by traffic type

Every figure below is measured per completed task with quality held (at least
36 of 40 tasks fully correct and complete), on a simulated harness using each
provider's published prices and cache rules — except where marked live. A
first real-traffic export exists (30 requests, measured 9–25% per agent);
your own pilot replaces every band with your number before any fee exists.
[How these numbers are made →](methodology.md)

| Your traffic looks like | Measured saving | Label |
|---|---:|---|
| Multi-turn Claude cache-only comparison | **37.6%** vs the same J prompt stack with cache disabled; both arms clean 38/40 | simulator-measured; cache effect isolated |
| Full J + 5m cache stack vs raw uncached baseline | **57.1% lower cost, −5 pp clean-task quality** | fails the agreed −2 pp quality limit; not a qualified win |
| Background / batch / latency-tolerant jobs | **57.7%** (net of assumed tier fallbacks; 64.3% ceiling) | simulator-measured |
| One-shot API calls on a shared template | **45.5%** — up to **72.8%** where latency-tolerant | simulator-measured |
| Interactive agents, sparse traffic | **34.0%** | simulator-measured, caveats apply |
| Interactive agents, busy traffic | **25.9–29.4%** | simulator-measured |
| Already-optimised stacks | **0–5% — do not pay us** | measured on fixtures |

The spread is the honest part: savings are a property of your workload's shape,
not of FLUX. The first thing FLUX does is tell you which row you are — from
your own logs, in about five minutes, before any contract exists.
[Get a quote from your own export →](../pilot/runbook.md)

## How it works, in one paragraph

Your bill is `tokens × price-per-token × execution tier`. FLUX attacks all
three at once: it removes tokens that carry no information (oversized tool
results capped at injection, exact duplicates, schema bloat) without ever
breaking your provider's prefix cache; it repairs prompts so cached pricing
(10× cheaper input) actually applies; and it routes traffic you flag as
latency-tolerant to the provider's own discounted tiers (50% off, same model,
same answer). Risky changes are enabled only after a replay gate proves, on
your own recorded requests, that quality held.

## Why you can trust the number on your invoice

- Savings are computed from your **provider's own reported usage**, never our estimates.
- Every request writes a **hash-chained ledger event**; your invoice is a pure
  function over those events that **you can recompute yourself**, to the cent.
- Savings you already had — your provider's cache, your gateway's cache — are
  itemised and **never billed**.
- A changed answer is a failed task, and **failed tasks void their savings**.

[Methodology](methodology.md) · [Per-segment detail](segments.md) ·
[Honest comparison with alternatives](comparison.md) · [FAQ](faq.md) ·
[Every number's provenance](evidence.md)

# What FLUX saves, segment by segment

Savings are a property of your workload's shape. One global percentage would be
a lie to someone; these are the four shapes, each with its mechanism, its
measured band, and what would change the number. All figures simulator-measured
per [methodology](methodology.md); traceability in [evidence](evidence.md).

## Background / batch / latency-tolerant work — 57.7% net (64.3% ceiling)

**Mechanism:** your provider sells the same model at 50% off for work that can
wait (OpenAI's flex service tier on a synchronous API; Anthropic's batches,
which stack with prompt caching). FLUX applies the tier only to traffic you
flag latency-tolerant, stacks it with every token lever below, and bills from
the tier the provider *actually served* — bounced requests bill at full rate.
**The number to use is 57.7%** (net of assumed 10% default-fallback + 5% retry
rates); 64.3% is the zero-fallback ceiling. Quality: identical model, identical
answers; 38/40 clean on the harness.
**What changes it:** your real fallback rate (telemetry replaces the
assumption), and Anthropic-side pricing once its batch rate is catalogued.

## One-shot API traffic on a shared template — 45.5%, up to 72.8%

**Mechanism:** the most common silent waste we model: a per-request value (a
timestamp, a request id) at the top of an otherwise identical prompt, which
disables provider caching entirely. FLUX relocates it, the prefix caches at
one-tenth price, and schema/duplicate levers stack on top. Add the tier for
latency-tolerant one-shots and the band reaches 72.8%.
**What changes it:** how big your shared template is and whether a breaker is
actually present — the five-minute quote measures both from your export.

## Interactive agents — 25.9–29.4% busy, 34.0% sparse

**Mechanism:** busy agent traffic is already heavily subsidised by the
provider's cache (35–40% on its own, which we never claim), so FLUX's honest
headroom is the *fresh* tokens: oversized tool results are capped at injection
(headlines, errors and file paths preserved verbatim; the replay gate approved
this lever at exactly zero quality delta), stale history is compacted
byte-stably, schemas are slimmed. Sparse traffic adds the 1-hour cache TTL
(2× write premium billed honestly, netted when negative) for 34.0%.
**What changes it:** how oversized your tool results actually are (our fixture's
are highly compressible; your yield scales with yours), and the pending
per-model cache-minimum fix, which may lower the sparse figure on some models.
**On Claude the ceiling is different — and higher.** Anthropic's prompt
cache is opt-in, and agents that never place `cache_control` re-pay full
rate for their whole conversation history every turn (our first live export
measured exactly that: a five-turn agent with zero cache traffic). FLUX
stamps the stable prefix with a 5-minute-TTL breakpoint. In the deterministic
fixture, the cache-only comparison is **37.6% lower cost** than the identical
J prompt stack with caching disabled; both arms have 38/40 clean tasks and the
stamp is metadata-only. The earlier **57.1%** full-stack comparison used a raw
uncached baseline with 40/40 clean tasks, while the candidate had 38/40 (−5 pp).
That fails the agreed −2 pp quality limit, so 57.1% is diagnostic and not a
qualified full-stack saving. Real-traffic cache validation remains open. If
you already place your own breakpoints, FLUX defers and never claims this.
**This is also where we tell you our ceiling:** if someone promises an
interactive agent 70%, ask for their per-task evidence.

## Already-optimised stacks — 0–5%: do not pay us

**Mechanism:** none, and that is the point. If your input already arrives
largely cached, or your gateway's response cache already answers a big share of
requests, FLUX's triage says so and the quote's verdict is `doNotPayUs`. On our
fixture of such a stack the addressable saving was 2.4%. A percentage-of-savings
vendor that charges you for savings you already had is buying a dispute; we
decline up front.

# Methodology — how every FLUX number is made

The LLM cost-saving market has a measurement problem, documented by independent
work rather than by us: three popular open-source token trimmers claiming
60–90% savings delivered **3.7%** when independently replayed over 614M tokens
of real traffic; a prompt-slimming technique modelled at ~77% measured **~13%**
in production. The gap comes from measuring per *request* instead of per
*completed task*, and from ignoring provider cache economics. FLUX's method
exists to be immune to both.

## The rules every published number passes

1. **Per completed task, not per request.** A technique that shrinks each
   prompt but multiplies round trips has saved nothing. Our harness runs
   multi-turn tasks end to end and prices the whole task.
2. **Quality held, measured.** A claimed arm must keep at least 36 of 40 tasks
   fully correct and complete. A changed tool call is a hard failure; a
   shortened answer is scored by degree. The simulated model's quality signal
   punishes trimming recent context — the fixture is built to catch our own
   levers failing.
3. **Provider cache rules simulated faithfully**: minimum cacheable prefix,
   longest-exact-prefix matching, hit granularity, time-to-live expiry, and
   write premiums. Our simulator can and does show caching as a **net loss**
   on unfavourable traffic — that case has a unit test.
4. **The provider's existing contribution is never claimed.** On busy agent
   traffic, the provider's cache alone saves 35–40% before FLUX does anything.
   That figure is printed separately and excluded from every FLUX claim.
5. **Tier savings are billed at the tier actually served.** Discounted-tier
   requests can be bounced back to full price under load; the published async
   figure (57.7%) is net of assumed fallback rates, and per-request billing
   reads the service tier from the provider's response, not from our request.
6. **Lossy levers pass a replay gate first.** Changes that could affect answers
   (description trimming, output caps, tool-result capping) are enabled only
   after replaying your recorded requests both ways, with statistics corrected
   for having searched multiple configurations. The gate has rejected our own
   levers — those rejections are documented, not tuned away.
7. **Unpriced means excluded, never zero.** A model or billing date the price
   catalogue cannot price is excluded from baselines and invoices, with the
   reason stated. Our catalogue is dated and source-linked; a price change
   never silently reprices history.
8. **The invoice is recomputable.** Every request emits an append-only,
   hash-chained event carrying provider-verbatim usage, the catalogue version,
   levers applied, and gate verdict references. `recomputeInvoice(events)` is a
   pure function: run it yourself and you must get our number.

## What "simulator-measured" means — and what it does not

All current figures come from a 40-task × 5-turn agent harness (plus one-shot
variants) with realistic multi-kilobyte tool results, verified by an
independent checker agent reproducing every number from command output, under
341 unit tests and 27 regression gates. They are honest measurements **of the
simulation**. They are not yet measurements of your traffic — the pilot exists
to produce that number, on your machine, from your logs, before you pay
anything.

Known open items we publish rather than hide: per-model cacheable minimums are
not yet in the simulator (the sparse-traffic 34.0% may overstate on some
models); Anthropic batch rates are not yet catalogued (the async figure is
OpenAI-priced); both are tracked in [evidence](evidence.md).

# Evidence — every published number, traced

Each figure on this site maps to the command that produces it and the commit it
was verified at. Reproduce any of them from the repo root. (Numbers were
independently re-verified by a checker separate from the implementer at each
listed commit; the harness run prints every row below.)

Harness: `node --import tsx evals/run-agent-ab.ts` · tests:
`./node_modules/.bin/vitest run` (341 passing) · gates: the three suites under
`evals/run-*-triage.ts` and `evals/run-analysis-regression.ts` against freshly
generated fixtures (27/27).

| Published figure | Where it comes from | Verified at |
|---|---|---|
| Async 64.3% ceiling / **57.7% net** (quote the net) | arm K rows, async-eligible segment: ceiling assumes 0% tier fallback; net assumes 10% default + 5% 429-retry, priced per event at the SERVED tier | `4e51734` |
| Interactive 25.9–29.4% | arm J across openai-30s / openai-600s / anthropic-5m blocks, clean 38/40 | `c7b03d4`, re-verified `4e51734` |
| Proxy mode: zero-code integration | `packages/sdk-js/src/proxy.ts` + `evals/run-proxy.ts`; e2e tests cover reduction-before-forward, byte-identical passthrough, SSE streaming with usage parsed after the last byte, per-app hash chains, credential passthrough | `d31b125` |
| SECOND live export: 18.0% of real spend, every active agent billing | `evals/run-live-agents.ts` keyed rerun with the 5m cache stamp + the freshcap gate verdict wired: coding-agent $0.0206 (cap+schemas net of a −$0.0063 cache miss from its per-turn clock), batch-classifier +$0.0101 (cache stamp EARNING live, 6,286 reads), rag $0.0086, support $0.0054, already-lean $0 | run 2026-10-19, spools audited in session |
| Multi-turn Claude cache-only comparison: 37.6% | `node --import tsx evals/run-cache-decomposition.ts` — J + 5m stamp vs the identical J stack with cache disabled; both arms clean 38/40, 96% hits, 200/200 stamps metadata-only. Isolates the pure cache effect | independently re-derived and reproduced 2026-10-19 |
| Full J + 5m stack vs raw uncached A: 57.1% lower simulated cost | same decomposition script, row 2: quality 38/40 vs the raw baseline's 40/40 (−5 pp; within the published >=36/40 gate, but a real delta) — quote 37.6% for the cache lever and label this one with its quality cost | `6249f86`, reproduced 2026-10-19 |
| Sparse interactive 34.0% | arm L, 1h cache TTL via the shipped `cacheTtl` stamp (stable-prefix placement), 600s spacing | `67eeac6` (re-verified after the placement fix `ec191c5`; was 34.0% at `cbbffb9`) |
| First real-traffic export: 9.3% net of spend | `evals/run-live-agents.ts`, 30 requests on claude-sonnet-5-5; a smoke run, NOT a band — lossy levers were recorded-unbilled and the old cache placement lost money (per-agent outcomes ranged −24% to +34% of that agent's spend) | `d84e256` run 2026-10-19, superseded by the second export |
| One-shot 45.5% / 72.8% | one-shot section, arms H and I ($0.569 → $0.310 / $0.155) | `7b08666`, re-verified `4e51734` |
| Provider cache's own 35–40% (never claimed by FLUX) | "what the cache itself is worth" section of the harness output | `33028df` onward |
| "Do not pay us" 0–5% | support-assistant fixture, 77% pre-cached, triage verdict | `ff04a70` |
| Replay gate approving fresh-cap at 0.00 quality delta and rejecting the 2000-token output cap at −5.50pp | `evals/run-replay-gate-freshcap.ts` | `ab5b4c7` |
| Ledger determinism, exclusions, recomputable invoice | `packages/core/src/savings-ledger.test.ts`; canonical-invoice contract | `597e842`, `10407bf` |

## Open items (also stated wherever the affected number appears)

- Per-model cacheable minimums not yet simulated → 34.0% may overstate on some
  models.
- Anthropic batch rate uncatalogued → async figures OpenAI-priced; Anthropic
  batch events are correctly *unpriced*, never zeroed.
- Package freshness gate and automated CJS smoke not yet in the build script
  (the CJS tarball was smoke-tested manually at `4e51734`).
- **The banded figures are simulator-measured.** A first real-traffic export
  exists (30 requests, see the table) and found one lever losing money on
  one-shot traffic — fixed at `ec191c5` and re-verified. The bands stay
  simulator-labelled until a pilot-scale export replaces them.

## Independent sources cited on the comparison page

- codepointer.dev — 614M-token replay of rtk/headroom/caveman: 3.7% actual.
- archestra.ai — progressive disclosure: ~77% modelled vs ~13% measured.
- RouterArena (arXiv:2510.00202) — independent router leaderboard.
- Anthropic & OpenAI published pricing pages — all rates in
  `packages/core/src/model-prices.ts` carry source URL and capture date.

# An honest comparison — including where FLUX loses

Most cost-saving tools publish their best number. Independent measurement keeps
finding a gap between claimed and delivered, so this page compares *methods*,
and includes the rows where we lose.

## The independent findings this market needs to answer

- Three popular open-source token trimmers (rtk, headroom, caveman), claiming
  60–90%, were independently replayed over a 614M-token corpus of real coding
  sessions: **3.7% combined actual saving** (codepointer.dev deep dive).
- Progressive disclosure of tool schemas, modelled at ~77% token savings,
  measured **~13% in production**, because the router it adds costs an extra
  round trip per novel tool call (archestra.ai bench). Per-request measurement
  cannot see this; per-task measurement can.
- The best-funded commercial router ranked **12th of 12** on the independent
  RouterArena leaderboard while advertising 30%+ savings.
- Our own history is on this page too: our first caching claim was 29%; our own
  per-task harness cut it to ~2% on busy agent traffic because the provider's
  cache was already doing the work. We published the correction and kept the
  gate that caught it.

## Method comparison

| | Typical trimmer / router | FLUX |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of measurement | per request | **per completed task** |
| Quality check | self-graded or none | replay gate on your recorded requests; failed tasks void savings |
| Cache economics | usually ignored (trimming can *raise* bills: one measured case cut tokens 38% and raised cost +6.8%) | simulated to provider rules; cache-safe levers only |
| Customer's existing savings | silently absorbed into the claim | itemised, excluded, never billed |
| Headline number | one global percentage | per-segment bands, including "do not pay us" |
| The invoice | trust us | hash-chained events; recompute it yourself |

## Where FLUX loses, stated plainly

- **Busy interactive agents: ~29% ceiling.** The provider's cache already
  delivers 35–40% there. Anyone promising such traffic 70% is claiming either
  the provider's savings or quality you will lose.
- **Already-optimised stacks: 0–5%.** Our triage will tell you not to buy.
- **A free trimmer may be all you need** if your waste is one obvious thing and
  you don't need the saving verified. FLUX's value is the *verified, billable*
  number; if you don't need that, rtk is free.
- **All current FLUX figures are simulator-measured.** The pilot exists to
  replace them with numbers from your own traffic before any fee applies.

## Not competitors: LiteLLM, Helicone, Langfuse

These are gateways and tracers — excellent at routing, logging and spend
tracking, and none of them performs token reduction or savings verification.
FLUX reads their exports directly: if you run any of them, you are one file
export away from a quote. [Runbook →](../pilot/runbook.md)

# FAQ — built from the caveats we already print

**Can FLUX break my app?**
The default levers are lossless: compacted schemas decode identically, removed
duplicates are exact, prefix repair reorders text without deleting it, and the
reducer never throws — any failure returns your request untouched. Lossy levers
(output caps, description trimming, tool-result capping) are off until a replay
gate proves on your own recorded requests that quality held.

**Why do you quote me a range and not one number?**
Because savings depend on your traffic's shape. The quote comes from your own
export and names your segment; a vendor quoting everyone one number is wrong
for most of them. Sometimes our verdict is literally `doNotPayUs`.

**Is 57.7% (async) real?**
It is a faithful measurement of a realistic simulation at providers' published
prices, net of assumed discount-tier fallback rates, with quality held at 38/40
clean tasks — and it is labelled simulator-measured everywhere it appears. Your
pilot replaces it with your own number before any fee exists.

**You're billing a counterfactual — how is that dispute-proof?**
The same way energy performance contracts have done it since 1995: a defined
baseline, provider-verbatim measurements, and an adjustment method agreed in
advance. Concretely: every request writes an append-only hash-chained event;
the invoice is a pure function over those events; you can re-run it and must
get our number. Savings you already had are itemised and excluded. Negative
savings (e.g. a cache-write premium that didn't pay off) reduce the bill —
they are never clamped to zero.

**Do I have to change my code?**
One line or none. SDK mode wraps your existing client (`withFlux(client)`).
Proxy mode needs no code at all: run the FLUX proxy locally and point your
client's `base_url` at it — your API key passes through verbatim (FLUX never
holds credentials), responses stream back untouched, and every request
appends the same hash-chained ledger event the SDK writes. A stream whose
usage cannot be read is recorded *unpriced*, never guessed.

**What do you do with my prompts?**
Analysis runs locally; prompts never leave your machine. The ledger records
usage numbers, lever names, hashes and verdict references — not prompt text.
One optional exception you control: the SDK can POST usage metadata (never
prompt text) to an endpoint **you configure yourself**; it is off unless you
set it. Full detail: [data handling](../pilot/data-handling.md).

**What if the provider changes prices?**
The price catalogue is dated and source-linked. A new rate is a new dated
entry; history is never silently repriced, and an uncovered date is "unpriced",
which excludes the row rather than guessing.

**What does it cost?**
1% of verified savings, monthly — nothing else. No subscription, no seats,
no minimum. A month that saved nothing bills nothing, and negative lever
months count against us.

**What's the catch?**
Three, published: busy interactive agents cap around 29% because the provider's
cache already does the heavy lifting; the 34.0% sparse figure awaits a
per-model cache-minimum correction and may come down for some models; Anthropic
batch pricing isn't catalogued yet, so the async figure is OpenAI-priced today.
When a number moves for honesty reasons, this site moves with it — the async
headline already went from 64.3% to 57.7% that way.
